questions.question: For an operation $\star$ on $A$, what does the arrow $\star:A\times A\to A$ guarantee about the output?
options: The operation is automatically associative.
The operation is automatically commutative.
The output may lie in any larger set containing $A$.
Every ordered pair of elements of $A$ is assigned an element of $A$.
questions.explanation: $\star:A\times A\to A$ guarantees that every ordered pair of elements of $A$ is assigned a single element of $A$.
questions.source_support: Definition: a binary operation on $A$ is a function $A\times A\to A$.

It does not make the operation commutative.
The output stays in $A$, not in a larger set.

questions.question: Why is closure not an extra theorem for a binary operation on $A$?
options: Because closure follows from commutativity alone.
Because every subset of $A$ contains all outputs.
Because the codomain is already $A$.
Because every operation on a set is associative.
questions.explanation: The codomain in $\star:A\times A\to A$ is already $A$, so closure ($a\star b\in A$) is built into the definition rather than a separate theorem.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: closure is built into the definition.

questions.question: Does the phrase “binary operation on $A$” by itself say that the operation is associative?

No. Associativity is an additional property that may or may not hold.
Yes, but only when $A$ has more than two elements.
questions.explanation: No — being a binary operation only requires a well-defined output in $A$; associativity is a separate property that may or may not hold.

questions.question: Why is subtraction on $\mathbb N$ a warning example for binary operations?

questions.question: On the set of positive real numbers, define $a\star b=a/b$. Is this a binary operation?
options: No, because division is not associative.
Yes; $a/b$ is positive when $a,b$ are positive.
No, because division is not commutative.
Only if $a=b$.
questions.explanation: Yes — for positive $a,b$, the quotient $a/b$ is again positive, so $\star$ maps $\mathbb R_{>0}^2\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ (closed), making it a binary operation.
questions.source_support: Definition: a binary operation only requires a function $A\times A\to A$.

questions.skill_detail: Separate closure from other algebraic properties.
option_explanations: Associativity is not the criterion for being a binary operation; only closure ($a/b\in\mathbb R_{>0}$) matters, and division is a binary operation on the positive reals despite being non-associative.
Commutativity is not required; a binary operation need not satisfy $a\star b=b\star a$, and division is non-commutative yet still a binary operation here.
It works for all positive $a,b$, not only when $a=b$; e.g. $6\star 2=3$ is a positive real, so $\star$ is defined on every pair.
